    The tools to prove consistency of Quine’s NF

    Murdoch J. Gabbay Heriot-Watt University [Edinburgh, UK]

    Abstract

    We give an account of the tools used in a recent proof of the consistency of TST+ (typed set theory with typical ambiguity). TST+ is equivalent to Quine’s New Foundations; both are type theories in which the ‘collection of all elements’ is an element of itself, whose consistency has been an open problem. These tools include a new cumulative hierarchy model based on an innovative ‘small support’ condition, a new category generalising the category of nominal sets, some surprising counting lemmas, and interesting sets bijections. The application to the consistency proof is given in accessible detail, suﬃcient to reconstruct the full proof.

    2012 ACM Subject Classiﬁcation Theory of computation Logic

    Keywords and phrases Foundations of computing, semantics with atoms, logics and type theories with universal set, Quine’s NF, nominal techniques

    1 Introduction

    Consider the following false reasoning: deﬁne . It is easy to check that if and only if . This is Russell’s paradox and is one of the central paradoxes of naive set theory.

    Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory (ZF) avoids paradox by insisting that be guarded; we can only form where is already known to be a set. We pay the price that we cannot form ‘reasonable’ sets such as the universal set (the set of all sets) or the set of ‘all sets with 2 elements’.1

    New Foundations (NF) avoids paradox by insisting on a stratiﬁable language [11]. In a stratiﬁable syntax, every variable and term can be assigned a level in such that we only form if level( level()1. So and are outlawed because no matter how we assign levels, level() can never be equal to level()1.

    The example expressions univ and 2 above are stratiﬁable, and are valid in NF. See the discussions in [1] and [8], and the clear summary with bibliography in [2]. One feature of NF is that it has a universal set (so the universe is an element, and is an element of itself), so NF does not need any hierarchy of universes as is often seen in foundations without a universal set.

    If NF is obscure in computer science compared to HOL and ZF, this must be in part because it was not known consistent.2 A proof of the consistency of Quine’s NF (ConNF) using powerful generalisations of nominal techniques is presented in [4]. That paper, which is under review, is technical and aimed as it has to be at the reader expert in set theory and very interested in ConNF.

    However, the proof contains several new ideas which I think may merit a broad audience. This paper provides an accessible introduction to these ideas, and highlights the tools more from a computer science (rather than a pure set theorist or NF-iste) point of view; see the list below. This paper started as a companion to the proof in [4] but has become an independent research contribution: most notably with the introduction of the category PART and the powerset object functor, and how this paper brings out the mathematical tools used in the proof in a new way. These tools include:

    1. A generalisation of nominal ‘ﬁnite support’ to ‘small partition support’ (Deﬁnition 3.9).

    2. A sets hierarchy with non-increasing cardinality (Deﬁnition 3.17; Theorem 3.18).

    3. The category PART of uniformly partitioned sets (Deﬁnition 4.9).

    4. The power object functor on PART (Deﬁnition 4.15), and the surprising fact that it preserves the ﬁrst-order structure of sets (Theorem 4.23).

    5. The technical but elegant ‘squashing lemmas’ of Subsection 4.5.

    Our presentation is optimised for readability, while including enough information to reconstruct the technical details in [4]. The proof considered in this paper is of a theory TST+ (deﬁned below), which is equiconsistent with NF by a result of Specker [13].

    2 The language of stratiﬁed sets and TST+

    2.1 Syntax and axioms

    Definition 2.1

    The language of TST+ is ﬁrst-order classical logic with a binary predicate , and:

    Remark 2.4

    In condition 2 of Deﬁnition 2.1, terms and can only be variable symbols. While suﬃcient in principle, for usability we may prefer richer term languages. Two will interest us here:

    We may wish to permit constants from a model, once we have built it. See Deﬁnition 5.1.

    We may wish to permit explicit comprehension . If so, we set level( level()1.

    Explicit comprehension terms add no expressivity to TST+, because of the Comprehension axiom, but it is natural and convenient. I call this syntax the language of stratiﬁed sets: in [5] we study it from the point of view of rewriting theory and prove it conﬂuent and strongly normalising — just like the simply typed -calculus, a syntax to which it is closely related, as we now discuss.

    2.2 Connection to Higher-Order Logic

    A connection between TST and Higher-Order Logic (HOL; simply-typed -calculus with base types individuals and booleans ) may be worth mentioning.

    Consider TST with explicit comprehension terms and deﬁne a mapping from TST levels to HOL types, and TST terms and predicates to HOL terms, as follows:

    Deﬁne hol and hol( hol() for 1.

    Biject level variables of TST+ with type hol() variables of HOL. For simplicity take this to be equality, so if level( in TST+ then : hol() in HOL.

    Suppose 1 and level( and is a TST+ predicate. Deﬁne hol(hol().

    Other connectives map unchanged, e.g. hol(hol() and hol(hol().

    Under this translation the comprehension axiom [:] maps to -equality () [:], and the sets extensionality axiom maps to function extensionality.

    Thus TST can be viewed naturally as a subsystem of HOL (this has not been noted in the NF literature, as far as I know). TST+ extends with typical ambiguity, which is not a HOL property. One way to model typical ambiguity would be to exhibit a bijection between the types hol() and hol( hol() for every 1; clearly this would suﬃce to prove . Unfortunately, this is impossible by a diagonalisation argument, at least if we interpret as ‘all functions’.

    So from the point of view of the translation above, the diﬃculty in proving the consistency of TST+/NF comes from ﬁnding a way to model typical ambiguity without running foul of diagonalisation. In a nutshell, we do this by restricting to small partition supported sets, then layering uniformly 1-partitions on top of this restriction, and ﬁnally bijecting hol(1) with hol(). Notation follows.

    Theorem 5.7

    TST+ is consistent.

    Proof

    The hierarchy ( 1) from Deﬁnition 3.17 is a model: Extensionality is a fact of sets. Comprehension is Proposition 5.5. For typical ambiguity, we reason as follows:

    1. By Theorem 3.18 we have a bijection : .

    2. We choose some uniform 1-partition on , and using it we present as an object in PART.

    3. We transfer this partition along to , and present as an object in PART.

    4. We obtain a bijective arrow : PART. ‘ bijective’ here means something speciﬁc, and is partial on underlying sets in a very speciﬁc way (Notation 4.22); this partiality is what helps sidestep diagonalisation counterarguments.

    5. Using Theorem 4.23 we repeat and extend this to a sequence of bijective arrows in PART between and for every 2.

    6. By the ﬁrst squashing lemma Lemma 4.17, if a witness exists to some in the language of stratiﬁed sets — where mentions only variables no lower than level 2; along with ﬁnitely many constants from (so also no lower than level 2) and supported by () for some — then is also a witness (), so that it is in the domain of our bijections.

    7. We are now essentially done, because we know that if an existential witness exists at a ‘high’ level, then one exists at a ‘lower’ level. Typical ambiguity follows by induction on predicates.

    Remark 5.8

    We have elided a technical detail: the hierarchy in Deﬁnition 3.17 imposes small partition support conditions on for every smaller . We should check that preserves these symmetries. It does. The proof is by diagram-chasing computations, checking that permutations commute as they should. The relevant calculations are in Subsection 6.2.3 and Subsection 6.3 of [4].

    6 Conclusions

    ZF, HOL6, and NF/TST+ are cousins: they arose contemporaneously in response to Russell’s paradox.

    If NF/TST+ has been less studied than ZF and HOL7 this may partly be because ZF and HOL have cumulative hierarchy models (as featured in many an undergraduate course on mathematical foundations). NF and TST+ had no such model, and indeed no models were known at all, and indeed NF and TST+ were not known consistent. It makes sense why powerful computer science tools have so far been based on derivatives of ZF and HOL, but not NF.

    We have studied NF using ideas from computer science in general and from nominal techniques in particular (as presented in e.g. [6, 10, 3]); and bringing to bear this combination of ideas along with new ones, we have proposed a model for TST+ (Deﬁnition 3.17). Furthermore, this is not just any model: it is a cumulative hierarchy model — like the ZF cumulative sets hierarchy model — and thus is a natural model for an extensional theory.

    If the TST+ cumulative hierarchy from Deﬁnition 3.17 is more complex than the ZF sets hierarchy, with its small partition support conditions, well: this buys new bijections, limits cardinalities, and gives us typical ambiguity and a universal set,8 and lets us model a stronger theory.

    The tools described in this paper are hard, but in interesting ways: small partition support (Deﬁnition 3.9), the power object functor (Deﬁnition 4.15), and uniform partitions (Subsection 4.2) are new ideas, with good behaviour (like the squashing lemmas in Subsection 4.5, and Theorem 4.23) and they serve a nontrivial application (build a model of TST+ and so prove ConNF). Future work includes applying these ideas to devise more structured type theories with universal sets, including constructive ones; TST+ is the case of a classical theory in which types are just .
